note: Both hold that carefully labelled legal training data is scarce or costly, and one offers case-law citations as a stand-in supervision signal where no such data exists.
The strategy of creating training data efficiently from pre-existing legal cases is instantiated by learning relevance from the citations already present in case law.
Both hold that hand-built rules cover part of a legal task but are costly or brittle, and that learned models should complement them.

One states that legal NLP has few large-scale systematic resources; the other presents a two-million-decision database with an extracted citation network as a significant training resource — the tension dissolves if 'systematic resource' means an annotated benchmark rather than a raw corpus.

Both attribute the shape of legal NLP methods to the scarcity of large labelled legal training data, one explaining why summarisers stay extractive and unsupervised, the other why statutory-reasoning data is costly to build.
Both state that the legal domain lacks large-scale training resources.

One says large training data is lacking in the legal domain; the other presents a two-million-decision database as a significant training dataset — compatible if 'training data' means task-labelled data such as summaries rather than raw corpora.
Both report that automatically identified legal key terms (catchphrases; Black's Law Dictionary terms) match or exceed what legal experts select.
Forum posts with poster-supplied flairs supply labelled legal data without lawyer annotation, which answers the cost problem the other claim states.
Both concern the scarcity of legal NLP resources; one names public legal forums as an underexplored large data source.
Both report legal-domain adaptation of BERT-type models failing to help on some legal tasks, for different stated reasons (informal input text; task not exercised by pre-training).

One finds a case-law-adapted BERT much better adapted to legal queries; the other finds LEGAL-BERT worse and less stable on informal legal questions — reconcilable if adaptation helps only on formal legal text.
Reducing the amount of labelled data needed addresses the expense of lawyer-annotated legal training data that the other claim states.
Both state that annotated legal resources are few; one for legal NLP at large, the other for rhetorical-role corpora.
Both hold that producing labelled legal data is hard because it demands legal expertise; one adds that even experts disagree.
Self-training on abundant unlabelled judgments is one mechanism for the efficient creation of training data from pre-existing legal cases that the other claim calls for.
Both propose ways to reduce the amount of expert-labelled legal data required (self-training; parameter-efficient few-shot adaptation).
Both attribute LEGAL-BERT's uneven transfer to the composition of its pre-training corpus (EU legal documents; formal legal text).
Both find that legal-domain pre-training of BERT gives little or no gain on the task at hand.
Both hold that outcome prediction improves when it proceeds through legally meaningful intermediate units of the case text (rhetorical roles; ascribed factors) rather than from raw text.

One predicts that straightforward application of a large-scale language model will not improve SARA performance; the other reports that straightforward GPT-3 prompting beats the previous BERT-based state of the art on SARA. The later source cites the earlier one only for the dataset, not on this prediction, so the edge is inferred.
Both characterise statutory reasoning as applying natural-language legislative rules to facts and treat it as a basic, real-world reasoning task.
Both find that models fail to use the statutory text supplied to them properly — BERT-type models ignoring it, GPT-3 citing the wrong subparagraph even with the statute in the prompt.
Both present statutory reasoning as a task that should motivate further model development.
Both hold that hand-encoding legislation into a formal representation demands legal expertise and time, and that automating it is an open problem.
LLM extraction of criteria-and-conclusion pathways from legislation is an instance of the strategy of automatically extracting structured rule knowledge from statutory text.
Both report that a GPT model working on statutory text makes structural or reference errors that prompt instructions and in-prompt statute text only partly prevent.
Denying the antecedent (inferring conclusions the article does not license) and concluding that a statute applies when it does not are both over-inference errors of a GPT model on statutory rules.

One finds that supplying the legislative text in the prompt viably constrains the model's textual output to that text; the other finds GPT-3 still refers to the wrong part of a statute when the statute is in the prompt — the tension dissolves if textual fidelity and correct cross-reference are distinct.
Both envisage the AI system augmenting a legal expert who verifies its output rather than replacing that expert.
Both hold that the ambiguity or open texture of statutory language is itself an obstacle to automated processing of statutes.

One questions the feasibility of classifying legal outcomes from fact descriptions alone after humans performed at chance; the other reports a fine-tuned BERT reaching macro F1 66.5 on ECHR violation prediction from case facts — above chance, though on a different task formulation.
Both move away from end-to-end fact-to-outcome prediction: one doubts its feasibility, the other assigns machine learning the role of identifying factors rather than predicting outcomes.
One calls for retrieval of key precedents to improve verdict classification; the other builds a system that predicts which sources of law are relevant to a given legal text.
One argues that AI legal classifiers need human benchmarks across experience levels; the other reports a lawyer baseline alongside model scores on legal-term identification.
Both find that supplying the relevant legal text in the prompt (a curated knowledge base; the statute) raises a GPT model's accuracy on legal questions.
Both report that grounding the prompt in the authoritative legal text improves the fidelity or accuracy of LLM output.
Both hold that LLMs' legal knowledge or advice is partly wrong on closer inspection despite headline successes.
Both temper LLMs' headline legal successes with evidence of unsound outputs on basic legal work.
Both expect an AI system answering legal questions to extend legal help to those who lack expertise or cannot afford it.
Both find that legal-domain-specific pre-training confers no advantage over fine-tuning general pre-trained models on the task at hand.
Both report legal-specific pre-trained models underperforming other approaches on their tasks.
Both observe that legal-specific pre-training (LEGAL-BERT and similar) gives at best mixed gains over general models.
Both report that performance of legal NLP systems varies across legal sub-domains, attributing it to low overlap or small domain-specific data.

One finds human legal experts substantially outperforming all models at predicting tribunal outcomes from facts; the other finds human performance at classifying court outcomes from facts no better than random — different courts, tasks and participant expertise.
Both assert, as a general methodological point, that AI outcome predictors need a collected human performance reference for meaningful comparison.
Both report fine-tuned pre-trained transformers outperforming zero- or few-shot large language models on a legal classification task.

One finds fine-tuned transformers beating prompted GPT models on outcome prediction; the other finds prompted GPT-3 beating the fine-tuned BERT-based state of the art on statutory reasoning — opposite rankings on different tasks.
Both find that putting task-relevant legal material (similar cases; a curated knowledge base) into the prompt improves LLM accuracy.
One calls for adding references to related cases to improve outcome prediction; the other finds that similar-case examples in the prompt improve it.
Both find that the cases or labels on which human experts disagree or struggle are also the ones on which models perform worst.
Both hold that fact descriptions available to the predictor may lack elements needed to determine the outcome.

One warns that facts extracted from judges' post-decision texts may carry information bias; the other defends post-decision material as the input that lets inaccuracies be attributed to the predictor's judgment.
Both use automation (LLM annotation; self-training) to reduce the burden of expert manual annotation of legal documents.
LLM annotation is offered as a way around the expense of lawyer-made training data that the other claim states.
Both distinguish outcome prediction from outcome classification by whether outcome information is present in the input material.

Santosh et al. cite Mumford et al. (2023b) — 'human performance on the judgment prediction task closely resembled randomness' — as one of the converging results that cast doubt on the benchmark-performance assumption, situating the finding alongside Branting et al. (2021).
The same citation of Mumford et al. (2023b) reports that human performance 'was unaffected by domain knowledge' and treats it as evidence within the paper's argument.
Both call for combining knowledge-based legal models with learned components; one proposes exactly such a hybrid.
Both hold that rules or expert knowledge and machine learning should complement each other rather than one replacing the other.

One warns against assuming legal expertise will emerge from data alone and urges integrating expert knowledge; the other presents learned dense representations replacing explicit logical structure as the adaptable alternative to hand-built solvers.
Both hold that statistical classifiers of legal outcomes fail to provide the kind of justification legal practice requires.
One argues binary outcome targets are reductive; the other finds that distinguishing partial wins from outright wins makes prediction much harder than the aggregated binary task.
Both question what classification benchmarks on fact descriptions actually measure about legal outcome prediction.
Both hold that fact descriptions taken from judgments are tailored to the decision and can bias outcome prediction.
One recommends pre-proceeding inputs such as party memoranda; the other identifies the information bias of judge-written facts that such inputs would avoid.
One says outcome prediction should rely on information available before proceedings; the other defends post-decision material as the appropriate input for a human verdict-classification study.
Both identify change in the law over the period covered by training data as an unaddressed source of prediction error.
Both hold that LLMs can semi-automate the construction of rule-based legal structures, easing the knowledge acquisition bottleneck, with humans verifying the result.
Both name the manual encoding of legal knowledge as the bottleneck that LLM-assisted structure extraction addresses.
One calls automatic generation of hand-built solvers an open question; the other reports LLMs beginning to answer it while leaving the correctness of the resulting structures open.
Both hold that benchmark metrics alone are insufficient and that human or expert references are needed to evaluate legal NLP systems.
Both call for evaluation of legal AI against human performance rather than convenient benchmark metrics alone.
Both characterise knowledge-based legal reasoning systems as faithful but dependent on scarce expert modelling effort.
Both describe the expert-effort bottleneck of building knowledge-based legal systems.
Both hold that argumentation or outcome support should rest on structured legal representations combined with learned text processing.
Both contrast LLMs' bar-exam successes with their weaker performance on other legal tasks.
Both report prompted LLMs scoring modestly on case outcome classification benchmarks.
Both temper LLMs' headline legal-exam results with poor performance on other basic legal reasoning tasks.
Both hold that AI should augment human legal decision makers rather than replace them.
Both envisage AI as support for a human expert who retains responsibility for the result.
Both assign text processing the role of ascribing factors from case text, leaving inference to a formal legal model.
The factor-ascription-then-formal-inference route described in one is the architecture proposed in the other.
Both find value in routing outcome prediction through legally meaningful intermediate units extracted from the text.

Both assert, as a general normative claim, that what a legal decision needs is an explanation of why it is the proper application of the law, capable of persuading and withstanding appeal, which fact-based prediction or word-level explanation does not supply.
Both note that AI and Law results and assumptions are tied to a particular legal tradition and may not carry across traditions.

One observes that AI and Law work reasons from a civil- or common-law background; the other explicitly reasons from India's common-law system in designing its corpus — an instance of the observed pattern.
Retrofit pair: both note that features of the legal tradition they work in (civil-code drafting for lay readability; common-law judicial discretion) shape what their method or data can support.
Both hold that building carefully annotated legal evaluation or training data is very resource-intensive, which keeps such datasets small.
Both use a large language model as the judge of another system's legal-text output and find it workable.
One reports LLM-based evaluation of legal summaries correlating well with human judgment; the other operationalises GPT-4 as an examiner of legal answers.
Both find encoder-type models trained or sized for short inputs unsuited to long legal texts.
Both find that tools built on non-legal text handle legal documents poorly because of their length, structure and reasoning.
Both hold that the complexity of legal text makes standard text-processing units and techniques inadequate for it.
One states legal NLP has few systematic resources; the other releases what it presents as the first meta-evaluation dataset for long-form legal summaries.
One treats temperature 0 as securing reproducibility; the other finds leading models unstable on identical inputs even at temperature 0 with every determinism parameter set.
Both document variability of GPT-family answers on legal questions — across prompt settings in one, across identical repeated calls in the other.
Both guard against training-data contamination of legal test material, one by checking the model's recognition of the benchmark, the other by changing names in distilled cases.
Both mask identifying names in legal test data to stop models exploiting memorised or overfitted identities.
Both report near-chance agreement with the court's actual outcome when predicting from a distilled description of a hard case.
Both report LLMs performing only modestly when judged against actual case outcomes.
Both suspect that a condensed description of a case, produced after the fact, can bias what a predictor concludes.
Both identify the summarised or selective form of the case description as a possible confound in outcome prediction.
Both counsel against direct real-world legal application of current LLMs, one from instability, the other from accountability.
Both draw doubts about using LLMs for real legal work from measured shortcomings on legal questions.
Both find general-purpose pre-trained models outperforming legal-domain-specific ones on a legal task.
Both find that restricting or adapting a model to legal text gives no advantage on the legal task measured.
Both report that legal-domain pre-training yields at best mixed gains against general models.
Both find that human-assigned legal labels, even from experts or court staff, carry inconsistency that limits their use as gold standards.
Both find BERT-type encoders limited by their 512-token window when embedding long legal documents, with windowing a partial remedy at best.
Both motivate similar-case retrieval by the burden and limits of existing legal search for practitioners.
Both report that reviewing an LLM's output exposed errors in the human annotations or reasoning it was compared against.
Both tie machine classification of laypersons' legal problems to timely access to legal help.
Both see AI triage of legal problems as a route to legal help for those otherwise underserved.
Both hold that bias in deployed legal AI must be examined because of its consequences for equal treatment or fair allocation of legal help.
Both motivate court-facing NLP tools by India's case backlog and long records, and see technology as easing rather than replacing judicial work.
Both hold that LLM output for legal users should be grounded in trusted source material rather than free generation.
Both constrain an LLM's output to the authoritative document supplied to it as the way to keep it verifiable.
Both address the time court staff and judges spend locating relevant material, one measuring the reduction a navigation tool brings.
Both envisage AI increasing what a judge can process under time constraints while the judge keeps control.
Both hold that AI in adjudication should preserve the human decision maker's control and transparency.
One finds retrieval into the prompt improves accuracy; the other notes retrieval reduces but does not eliminate hallucination — improvement without guarantee.
Both find that instructing an LLM (to abstain; to avoid a logical error) succeeds only partially, so guarantees are unavailable.
One documents the non-determinism of LLM answers; the other designs a grammar-first router precisely to keep courtroom command handling predictable, with the LLM only as back-off.
Both report erratic LLM behaviour with practical consequences — behavioural anomalies in dealmaking, unstable answers to legal questions.
Both counsel caution before delegating consequential decisions to current LLMs, on the basis of measured unreliability.
Both hold that consequential decisions should not be handed over to AI agents without human care or accountability.
Both find that the same LLM gives materially different answers to the identical legal question across repeated queries.
Both treat the variability of LLM answers as undermining their use as evidence or advice in legal settings.
Both find LLM answers on legal questions sensitive to how, or how insistently, the question is put.
Both hold that the closed, proprietary nature of leading LLMs prevents users from knowing what the model actually does, defeating transparency and explanation.
Both deny that results from proprietary LLMs are genuinely replicable.
Both hold that hallucination by LLMs cannot be fully cured by the remedies proposed for it.
Both hold that AI must not take over the judicial function of deciding; it may at most support the human judge.
Both reject full automation of judicial work in favour of tools that leave interpretation and decision to the judge.
Both counsel against relying on current LLMs for real legal determinations, citing their unreliability.

Waldon et al. quote Lee and Egbert approvingly ('we currently know next to nothing about the target language domain, operational domain, or sampling decisions behind the LLMs') and add their own account of non-naturalistic instruction and preference data as further reasons.
The same passage cites Lee and Egbert on LLM judgments not accounting for linguistic variables, and Waldon et al. add that fine-tuning data encode annotators' own linguistic judgments.

Waldon et al. discuss Lee and Egbert's 100-query study by name and argue that its risks 'are mitigated by setting random seeds when sampling', so that the demonstration is not a compelling challenge to careful direct querying.

Waldon et al. call Lee and Egbert's manipulation exchange 'not terribly surprising' and 'not terribly compelling to judges', since no judge would report an exchange that is on its face biased; they hold a compelling challenge must show misuse under robust conditions.
Both conclude that judges should not treat direct chatbot answers as evidence of ordinary meaning, though for partly different reasons.
Both counsel against relying on current LLMs for legal determinations because of their unreliability.
Both keep the human decision maker responsible, casting AI as a sparring or support role rather than an authority.
Both draw the line at outsourcing the interpretive judgment itself to an AI while allowing supporting uses.
Both hold that the opacity of what an LLM has learned bars responsible use of its outputs as evidence of meaning.
Both find that chatbot answers to legal questions are not reproducible across identical queries, one tracing it to hidden prompts and sampling, the other measuring it directly.
Both attribute the irreproducibility of proprietary chatbots to hidden, changeable components outside the user's view.
Both find that how a legal question is framed materially changes the LLM's answer.
Prompt shopping under robust, non-biased prompt variation is the stronger form of the manipulability that the other claim demonstrated under overt pushback.
Both hold that legal users over-trust LLM outputs, assuming determinism or authority the systems lack.
Both warn that the accessibility and apparent authority of chatbots invite uncritical judicial reliance.
Both prescribe fixed decoding settings (temperature, seed) and documented configurations as conditions of reproducible LLM experiments.
Both hold that closed, constantly changing proprietary models cannot be assessed or reproduced.
Both reject Judge Newsom's method of reading ordinary meaning off serial chatbot queries, one for its lack of experimental rigour, the other for its context-invariant premise.
Both describe textualist judges turning to corpus linguistics as an empirical tool of ordinary meaning.
One states in 2020 that legal NLP is growing but resource-poor; the other documents the sharp rise in shared datasets and code over 2013-2024 from that low base.
One reports a general-purpose model beating a domain-specific one on a legal task; the other frames the transferability of general models to law as real progress with open questions.
Both note general pre-trained models making real progress on legal tasks relative to legal-specific alternatives.
Both identify the complexity of legal language and documents as the principal barrier to effective legal NLP.
Both hold that legal text's complexity makes standard NLP techniques fall short.
One demands code and data with every publication for reproducibility; the other notes that results on proprietary models cannot be guaranteed reproducible.
Both treat replicability as requiring open methods and materials, not merely disclosed settings.
Both find GPT-family models improving on statutory or tax-law questions as models advance, beyond earlier systems.
One predicts that scaling language models will not straightforwardly improve statutory reasoning; the other reports accuracy on tax-law questions rising with each model release.
Both find chain-of-thought style prompting helps only inconsistently on legal questions, depending on model and setting.
Both find few-shot examples improve GPT-family accuracy on statutory questions.
Both find that supplying the relevant legal text to the model improves the accuracy of its legal answers.
Both find the statute or regulation in the prompt improves GPT performance on statutory questions.
Both find task-relevant legal material in the prompt raises LLM accuracy.
Both hold that current GPT models, though improving, fall short of expert legal competence.
Both temper LLM successes on legal questions with their remaining errors relative to professionals.
One expects superhuman legal skills to emerge as models advance; the other doubts GPT-3's ability to handle even basic legal work — a difference of outlook on the same trajectory.
Both generate novel synthetic legal test material so that it cannot have been in the model's training data.
Both alter or synthesise test material to defeat memorisation from training data.
Both use GPT-4 as an automated grader of legal answers and report it adequate.
Both find LLM-based judging of legal-text outputs workable after checking against human judgments.
Both report that the retrieval component of a legal RAG pipeline often fails to surface the relevant source.
Both expect LLM assistance to lower the cost of legal services and widen access.
Both envisage the LLM producing a first draft that a legal expert checks.
Both demand safeguards on bias and accountability before LLMs are deployed for legal work.
Both treat normative rules as defeasible — subject to exceptions and overriding conditions — and build that into how such rules should be represented.
Both aim to make AI systems act in accordance with legal and ethical norms — one by formal rules verified against the design, the other by law-informed model behaviour.
Both note that hand-written formal rule sets are error-prone and that small mistakes matter, which one addresses by automated conflict and redundancy checks.
Both find legal-task performance rising with model size or release, GPT-4 best.
Both rank GPT-4 above GPT-3.5 on legal tasks.
Both find smaller or open models matching commercial frontier models on some legal tasks.
Both treat an LLM's recall of legal rules as partial and error-prone — one measuring rule recall as a hallucination analogue, the other finding GPT-3 recites the tax code wrongly.
Both concern LLMs' inability to reproduce legal rules faithfully from memory.
Both find the choice of in-context examples materially changes LLM legal-task performance.
Both document large swings in LLM legal-task accuracy from prompt composition alone.
Both find that the wording of the task or question significantly affects LLM accuracy on legal tasks.
Both address benchmark contamination of commercial LLMs, one by warning of it, the other by generating novel test problems.
Both treat the possible presence of a public legal benchmark in LLM training data as a threat to evaluation validity.
Both hold that LLMs have likely seen public legal materials in training, which compromises evaluation on them.
Both hold that benchmark performance gives only a preliminary picture and that use-case-specific evaluation is required before deployment.
Both caution against drawing deployment conclusions from benchmark baseline scores.
Both warn that generalised benchmark results do not carry over to realistic legal tasks.
Both call for legal-domain evaluation designed around what practitioners recognise and need, rather than convenient metrics.
Both state that legal annotation is exceedingly expensive because it requires trained lawyers.
Both hold that legal data annotation demands scarce expertise.
Both note that building annotated legal evaluation data is resource-intensive and keeps datasets small.
Both note the heterogeneity of legal language across areas and document types as a challenge for models.
Both observe that legal model performance varies with the legal domain of the text.
Both catalogue characteristic LLM errors on legal rule application — misstating rules, arithmetic slips, wrong provisions.
Both find that stating the rule in the prompt can matter for rule-based legal questions, with effect varying by task.
Both report that supplying the governing rule text helps LLMs on some legal questions but not uniformly.
Both criticise existing legal benchmarks for reducing legal reasoning to coarse targets.
Both warn that harms from unreliable legal AI fall on the disadvantaged, motivating careful evaluation.
Both demand rigorous evaluation of legal AI given its potential harms and biases.
Both hold that feature- or word-level weight explanations are inadequate for legal text classification and that explanation should point to meaningful passages or reasons.
Both hold that producing fine-grained legal annotations is impractically expensive, which motivates label-free or weakly supervised methods.
Both derive additional supervision from a model's own outputs to avoid costly human annotation of legal text.
Both hold that generated legal summaries can misreport or omit legally decisive content, which is why one prefers anchored navigation and the other demands consistency checks.
Both document LLMs inventing or altering legal names, numbers and provisions in their output.
Both attribute a legal model's errors on one jurisdiction's documents to the jurisdiction of its training corpus.
Both explain a legal model's weakness on out-of-distribution legal text by the composition of its training data.
Both find legal case texts harder to summarise or match than non-legal documents.
Both hold that legal documents' length and complexity make them harder for NLP than ordinary texts.
Both identify legal language as a distinctive barrier lowering NLP performance relative to other domains.
Both hold that legal AI output should pass through a human expert rather than be deployed fully automatically.
Both envisage the LLM's output as a draft that a legal expert monitors and corrects.
Both counsel against unsupervised real-world use of current LLMs in legal settings.
Both treat the length of judgments as the defining difficulty of legal summarisation.
Both find that splitting long legal documents into model-sized chunks is a necessary but lossy workaround.
Both note the absence of prior systematic work on LLM-based long-form legal summarisation and its evaluation.
Both find general-domain models without legal training performing well on a legal task.
Both find that the retrieval component of a legal question-answering pipeline misses relevant sources and returns irrelevant ones.
Both report legal retrieval pipelines failing to surface the governing provisions.
Both observe that an LLM can give contradictory legal answers to the same or near-identical question across sessions.
Both find LLM legal answers sensitive to small changes in input.
Both note that chatbot answers vary across sessions and are therefore hard to reproduce.
Both design the interface to show the source passage or article grounding each output so that the user can verify it.
Both keep a human in the loop to correct or select what the AI system produces or retrieves.

One holds that a general-purpose embedding model lacks the legal knowledge needed to retrieve legal texts; the other finds a general-purpose embedder outperforming a domain-specific encoder on legal case retrieval.

One finds legal-domain fine-tuning of an embedding model significantly improves case retrieval; the other finds a general embedder beating a domain-trained encoder — reconcilable if fine-tuning a general model differs from training a small domain model from scratch.
Both benchmark many LLMs on legal tasks and find GPT-4 best while still far from satisfactory.
Both find GPT-4 the strongest model yet short of the level legal practice requires.
Both find legal-specific models failing to beat general models on legal tasks.
Both report general-purpose models matching or beating domain-specialised ones on legal tasks.
Both find legal-domain adaptation yielding no reliable advantage on the legal task measured.
Both report mixed results for legal-domain pre-training relative to general models.
One identifies change of law over time as neglected in legal NLP; the other measures LLMs failing at legal evolution tasks.
Both treat the evolution of legal norms over time as a source of model error.
Both find few-shot examples yield only slight gains on legal tasks.
Both find the effect of in-context examples on legal tasks unstable and model-dependent.

Both find LLMs weak at recalling or memorising legal knowledge, treating it as a fundamental limitation.
